impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model of expected function calls are directed to an abstract idea under step one of the Alice patent eligibility framework.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia University, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are abstract at step one of Alice and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on foreign sales were improperly awarded and reversed a contempt finding against Norton's counsel Quinn Emanuel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants in patent infringement cases involving software and cybersecurity patents a stronger basis to challenge eligibility under § 101, and limits damages exposure from foreign sales of accused products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in cybersecurity and software detection technologies face heightened invalidity risk under Alice, potentially undermining portfolios built around anomaly-detection methods.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL of invalidity for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112 for patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL of invalidity of Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments, after a jury had found willful infringement by Eli Lilly. The case involves Teva's Ajovy product and Lilly's competing migraine treatment, with billions of dollars in pharmaceutical market share at stake.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens pharmaceutical patent holders' ability to defend genus claims for antibody treatments where the specification discloses methods of making and using the claimed antibodies, even if only one specific embodiment is disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug manufacturers face continued patent barriers to entry in the lucrative anti-CGRP migraine treatment market.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licensed exclusive commercialization rights to a licensee but retained the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights retains sufficient standing under Article III to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement—along with rights to approve sublicenses, approve assignments, and practice the patents for R&D—retains sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy constitutional standing requirements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can retain enforcement rights and still maintain standing to bring infringement suits, providing flexibility in licensing and monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential jurisdictional defense when patent owners have carefully structured license agreements to retain meaningful exclusionary rights.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that four asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether ideas that are generally known in the art can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation and breach-of-contract claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law. The court also reversed on patent inventorship, holding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting liability and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that trade secret plaintiffs must present legally sufficient evidence of secrecy and independent economic value, protecting businesses from overbroad trade secret claims based on generally known information.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher evidentiary bar to sustain jury verdicts; companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust documentation of what makes their information truly secret and valuable.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality grounds where the accused multi-core processor selection method occurs partly outside the United States, and whether the court properly struck damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's '836 patent against Intel, finding that the extraterritoriality analysis was improperly resolved at summary judgment. The court affirmed the striking of certain damages expert theories for failure to adequately disclose them in damages contentions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against global technology companies receive clarification on when extraterritoriality defenses can be resolved at summary judgment versus trial, potentially expanding enforcement reach.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face uncertainty about extraterritoriality defenses to patent infringement, and must carefully manage discovery disclosure of damages theories to avoid exclusion.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's summary judgment of eligibility was proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations but affirmed eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed infringement and damages findings, including the denial of JMOL of non-infringement and the admission of Constellation's damages expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Confirms that patent claims incorporating specific technical implementations of communication technologies (such as specific constellation designs tied to hardware) can survive § 101 challenges, supporting IP monetization in the wireless standards space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement liability; abstract claims covering mathematical optimization of signal constellations remain vulnerable to § 101 challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify at summary judgment about matters outside their personal knowledge to establish the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) deposition testimony from a corporate representative who lacked personal knowledge of prior sales was admissible at summary judgment. The court also held that source code commands are not hearsay statements, though descriptive comments within code may be.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases gain a powerful tool for proving prior art sales through 30(b)(6) witnesses even when employees with personal knowledge are unavailable, and can use source code directly as non-hearsay evidence of product functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar invalidity challenges based on corporate representative testimony about historical product sales, even when the witness has no firsthand knowledge.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact preclude summary judgment on inequitable conduct during patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim for attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct (which had been granted to the patent challenger) and Walker Process fraud (which had been granted to the patent holder), finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The case involves coiled tubing patents where the patentee acquired prior art documents from its predecessor and allegedly failed to disclose them during prosecution.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct receive protection from summary judgment where factual disputes exist about intent to deceive the PTO; patent holders facing Walker Process claims also benefit from the same factual scrutiny.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire prior art through corporate acquisitions face significant litigation risk if they fail to disclose relevant predecessor documents during prosecution, with potential antitrust liability under Walker Process.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to a pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol (Veletri) patents by Mylan's proposed generic drug, holding that 'a pH of 13 or higher' is measured at a temperature standard in the field. The court also upheld the ruling that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine-of-equivalents infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from clear construction of pH-related claim limitations in pharmaceutical patents, facilitating ANDA filings and generic market entry for epoprostenol products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies holding composition patents with pH limitations face narrower claim scope, reducing their ability to block generic competition through both literal and equivalents theories.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated § 337 by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable pulse oximetry devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated § 337 by importing and selling Apple Watches incorporating blood oxygen functionality covered by Masimo's patents. The court upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models, finding no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in wearable health technology gain strong enforcement precedent through ITC proceedings, with the ability to obtain exclusion orders blocking importation of infringing consumer electronics products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies integrating health-monitoring features into consumer devices face significant import exclusion risk when those features are covered by competitors' patents, potentially requiring costly redesigns or licensing agreements.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion by excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated the summary judgment for Microsoft based on absence of a remedy. The court held that the district court applied an overly rigid standard in excluding the damages analysis related to virtual network optimization patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more flexible standard for admissibility of damages expert reports, reducing the risk that Daubert exclusions will eliminate the possibility of proving damages entirely.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits face continued exposure to damages claims even where the plaintiff's initial damages methodology was found wanting, as courts must allow opportunities to cure deficiencies.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the deadline for seeking a stay of the originally filed action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that BioMarin could not obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled declaratory judgment action where BioMarin had missed the 30-day deadline to seek a stay of the original action. The court rejected BioMarin's attempt to circumvent the statutory deadline by waiting for the plaintiff to refile its complaint.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and technology companies filing declaratory judgment actions alongside ITC proceedings benefit from certainty that opponents cannot manipulate statutory stay deadlines by waiting for refiled complaints.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents must strictly comply with the 30-day deadline in § 1659(a)(2) to obtain a mandatory stay of parallel district court actions; failure to timely seek a stay cannot be cured by the opponent's refiling.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where the Board failed to adequately address the distinction between dependent claims requiring a 'predetermined time delay' for reporting sensor information and the cited prior art.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's finding that all challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious, finding that the Board failed to adequately address dependent claims requiring a 'predetermined time delay' for reporting. The court also addressed Qualcomm's filing of IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against a different party (Roambee) on the last day of Roambee's filing deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the court's requirement that the PTAB conduct particularized analysis of dependent claim limitations in IPR proceedings rather than sweeping them into broader obviousness findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Third parties filing IPR petitions targeting patents asserted against others face scrutiny regarding the timing and strategic nature of their filings, though the court declined to review the Board's decision not to terminate the proceeding.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded statutory authority by charging PACER fees to fund non-PACER expenses. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting objections that the settlement was inadequate.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides precedent supporting incentive awards to class representatives in government overcharge class actions, and validates the Little Tucker Act as a jurisdictional basis for class claims challenging excessive government fees.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly determined that Tineco's redesigned wet-dry surface cleaning devices did not infringe Bissell's patents after the original products were found to infringe and subject to an exclusion order.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's determination in full, upholding both the exclusion order against Tineco's original infringing products and the finding that Tineco's redesigned products did not infringe. The court also affirmed the finding that Bissell established a technical domestic industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies facing ITC exclusion orders can successfully redesign products to avoid infringement while maintaining market access; the decision provides a roadmap for design-around strategies in Section 337 investigations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who obtain ITC exclusion orders may find their enforcement value diminished when respondents successfully redesign products to avoid infringement findings on key claims.
